A.explanation: Speed cannot increase because the enlarged parachute makes upward drag greater than weight, so the resultant force is upward while motion is downward.

B.explanation: Upward drag exceeds weight so the skydiver slows while falling, and because drag depends on speed the upward resultant force and acceleration shrink as speed falls.

C.explanation: Speed does not increase and acceleration is not uniform because the drag force changes as the falling speed changes.

D.explanation: The speed does decrease, but acceleration is not uniform because the net upward force $F = D - W$ decreases as drag $D$ decreases with speed.

hints: Notice the starting condition: falling vertically with terminal velocity means weight $W$ equals drag $D$ and resultant force is zero just before the parachute opens.
Connect the fully opened parachute to a much larger frontal area, so at the same high speed the drag $D$ suddenly becomes much larger than $W$ and gives an upward resultant force.
Link the falling speed to the drag force: as the downward speed decreases, $D$ decreases, so the upward resultant force $D-W$ and the magnitude of acceleration $a = (D-W)/m$ also decrease.
walkthrough: Identify the initial state: at terminal velocity the forces are balanced, so $W = D$ and acceleration is zero while the skydiver is still falling fast.
Describe the sudden change: when the parachute opens fully the effective area increases sharply, so drag at that high speed jumps to $D > W$.
Use $F = ma$: the resultant force $F = D - W$ is now upward, so acceleration is upward while velocity is downward, meaning the falling speed must decrease.
Explain why acceleration is non-uniform: drag depends on speed, so as speed falls $D$ falls, $D-W$ gets smaller, and the magnitude of upward acceleration gets smaller.
Conclude the motion is still downward falling with decreasing speed and a changing upward acceleration. This is option B.
